slides.narration: Welcome to Book III, Chapter 21: Appendix A — An Algorithmic Diagnostic Desk Reference. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. In algorithms, beauty is not enough. Every procedure needs a specification, a correctness argument, a cost model, and a witness that lets us inspect behavior.

slides.narration: The learning target is not memorizing an algorithm name. Learners should be able to explain why the algorithm is correct, what input size or structure controls cost, and what output or trace proves the implementation followed the intended procedure. For Appendix A — An Algorithmic Diagnostic Desk Reference, listen for evidence words: invariant, prefix, frontier, order, stability, recurrence, heap property, visited set, or witness.

question.prompt: Why is passing one test not the same as proving an algorithm?
question.answer: A test samples behavior. A proof or invariant explains why the procedure works for the stated input domain; tests then serve as witnesses and regression guards.

slides.narration: Read the roadmap as a sequence from requirement to evidence. First we make the problem precise. Then we choose a representation or procedure. Then we identify the invariant or ordering rule. Finally we inspect output, tests, diagnostics, or measurements. This keeps data structures from becoming names to memorize and turns them into operational tools.

slides.title: Start with the observed disagreement
keyPoints: A wrong result, a resource failure, and a slow result call for different first questions.
When the value is wrong, reduce the input while preserving the failure and compare the public contract with the.

slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 21, treat Start with the observed disagreement as an algorithmic claim. A wrong result, a resource failure, and a slow result call for different first questions. When the value is wrong, reduce the input while preserving the failure and compare the public contract with the observed output. When an allocation fails, inspect the accepted size and ownership transition. When elapsed time is high, establish that the result is correct before interpreting performance. Changing a representation without identifying the violated requirement can hide one symptom while creating another. A useful incident record contains the input, expected property, actual observation, build configuration, source revision, and the smallest known reproduction. “The tree fails sometimes” is not a reproduction. “After inserting 4,2,6,5 and deleting 4, inorder traversal contains 4 again” identifies an operation history that can be traced through the ownership links. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. Ask what invariant is preserved, what state changes, why termination follows, what input size controls cost, and what output or diagnostic proves the implementation matched the specification.

slides.title: Use operation histories, not only snapshots
keyPoints: Many data-structure defects need a sequence of actions.
A tombstone bug requires insertion, collision, deletion, and a later lookup or update.
A tail-pointer bug may require removing the only node and then inserting another.
A circular buffer defect may appear only after several wraparounds with alternating full and empty states.

A circular buffer defect may appear only after several wraparounds with alternating full and empty states. Represent these histories as replayable operations. Save the random seed and the actual minimized sequence when a generated test fails. A seed alone is not always a durable reproduction across changes to the generator or its operation distribution. Keep the operation grammar small enough that the sequence can be read and edited by a person. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.title: Distinguish missing results from exceptional failures
keyPoints: An unsuccessful search is often an ordinary result.
An invalid vertex index is a rejected request.
Exhausted memory is an environmental failure.
Treating all three as the same empty return value prevents callers from choosing an appropriate response.

An invalid vertex index is a rejected request. Exhausted memory is an environmental failure. Treating all three as the same empty return value prevents callers from choosing an appropriate response. The chapter interfaces vary intentionally to illustrate these choices. Read each contract before combining functions. In the supplemental application, an unreachable target is printed as unreachable with a successful process exit. A malformed input is an error with a different exit code. The application does not reinterpret disconnection as a parser failure merely because no route can be produced. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.title: Keep four forms of evidence separate
keyPoints: A proof explains why a stated algorithm satisfies a property under assumptions.
A reference comparison checks agreement with another implementation.
A sanitizer run investigates exercised low-level behavior.
A benchmark records performance for a specified workload and environment.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 21, treat Keep four forms of evidence separate as an algorithmic claim. A proof explains why a stated algorithm satisfies a property under assumptions. A reference comparison checks agreement with another implementation. A sanitizer run investigates exercised low-level behavior. A benchmark records performance for a specified workload and environment. A strong engineering argument often uses all four, but none automatically replaces the others. For example, an invariant can establish that lower-bound search shrinks the interval correctly. Exhaustive small-vector tests can catch an implementation typo. Sanitizers can expose an out-of-bounds access in an executed path. A benchmark can compare repeated query costs after sorting. Reporting one of these as all four exaggerates what was established. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. Ask what invariant is preserved, what state changes, why termination follows, what input size controls cost, and what output or diagnostic proves the implementation matched the specification.

slides.title: Decide whether to keep a custom structure
keyPoints: A custom teaching implementation makes hidden mechanisms visible.
That is a learning benefit, not a reason to deploy it by default.
Before replacing a standard container, write down the required operation mix, size range, ownership constraints.
Include maintenance and verification costs in the decision.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 21, treat Decide whether to keep a custom structure as an algorithmic claim. A custom teaching implementation makes hidden mechanisms visible. That is a learning benefit, not a reason to deploy it by default. Before replacing a standard container, write down the required operation mix, size range, ownership constraints, iterator guarantees, failure behavior, and measured bottleneck. Include maintenance and verification costs in the decision. A fixed-capacity specialized queue may be appropriate when rejecting overflow is part of the protocol. A hand-written general tree may be inappropriate when its deletion, allocator behavior, exception guarantees, and long-term maintenance are unproven. The choice should follow requirements and evidence rather than the amount of code already invested. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. Ask what invariant is preserved, what state changes, why termination follows, what input size controls cost, and what output or diagnostic proves the implementation matched the specification.
